documents.title: NPF treat-to-target consensus statement plaque psoriasis

chunks.content: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC Bimekizumab is a humanised monoclonal IgG1 antibody that selectively inhibits interleukin (IL)-17F in addition to IL-17A, which has demonstrated superior efficacy versus placebo and was generally well tolerated up to 5 years in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) and 3 years in patients with psoriatic arthritis (PsA). Due to the chronic nature of axSpA and PsA, there is a need for treatments that can be used long-term by patients, with sustained efficacy and tolerability. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS Across phase IIb/III studies, bimekizumab exhibited a consistent and favourable safety profile in patients with axSpA and PsA, with a total bimekizumab exposure of >2000 and >2500 patient-years, respectively. Overall incidence rates of treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were comparable between axSpA and PsA cohorts, remaining stable over extended periods of treatment with bimekizumab. No new safety signals were identified in this analysis. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY Together with previously published safety data, these results support the long-term tolerability of bimekizumab treatment in both patients with axSpA and PsA. Introduction Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) and psoriatic arthritis (PsA) are chronic, inflammatory, immune-mediated diseases with overlapping clinical characteristics, including axial and peripheral joint inflammation, pain and reduced functional ability. While chronic inflammatory back pain is a hallmark of axSpA, patients with PsA are more likely to have psoriasis and experience predominantly peripheral manifestations. Patients may also develop extramusculoskeletal manifestations such as uveitis and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), which are more common in patients with axSpA than patients with PsA. Bimekizumab is a humanised monoclonal IgG1 antibody that selectively inhibits interleukin (IL)-17F in addition to IL-17A. IL-17A and IL-17F are key mediators of inflammation, which have been implicated in the pathogenesis of axSpA, PsA and psoriasis. Bimekizumab has previously demonstrated superior efficacy versus placebo in patients with axSpA and PsA. Bimekizumab has also demonstrated superior efficacy versus placebo and comparator IL-17 inhibitors (IL-17i), IL-12/23 inhibitors (IL-12/23i) and tumour necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFi) in patients with plaque psoriasis. Previously reported safety data from clinical studies in axSpA, PsA and psoriasis showed that bimekizumab was generally well-tolerated at doses of 160 mg every 4 weeks (axSpA and PsA) or 320 mg every 4 weeks or every 8 weeks (psoriasis), with a safety profile that was consistent with anti-IL-17 biologics, aside from an increased incidence of mild-to-moderate oral candidiasis (due to the roles of IL-17A and IL-17F in antifungal immunity at the oral mucosa). These findings are further supported by recent systematic literature reviews and meta-analyses, which have reported that bimekizumab ranked favourably among other biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs) and targeted synthetic DMARDs for efficacy outcomes in patients with axSpA and PsA, with a comparable safety profile. Continuous monitoring of treatment safety and tolerability in the long-term is essential to inform future disease management for axSpA and PsA. Investigation of the long-term safety and efficacy of bimekizumab in axSpA and PsA is ongoing in the open-label extension (OLE) studies BE MOVING and BE VITAL, respectively. Here, integrated safety data from phase IIb/III randomised clinical studies and their subsequent OLE studies are presented by indication (including up to 5 years of total bimekizumab treatment in axSpA and up to 3 years in PsA), to assess the longer-term safety profile of bimekizumab in patients with axSpA and PsA, respectively. A graphical summary of results is provided in . Methods Patient population Safety data were pooled from phase IIb/III studies of bimekizumab in axSpA and PsA and their respective OLE studies ( ). At the time of data-cut, all phase IIb studies and their OLEs, BE AGILE 2 and BE ACTIVE 2, were complete or patients had received their final scheduled dose of bimekizumab (total of 5 years for axSpA and 3 years for PsA; ). Patients in the phase III randomised controlled studies had completed the final study visit, although some were awaiting safety follow-up. The OLEs, BE MOVING and BE VITAL, were ongoing for patients with axSpA and PsA, respectively. Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years and clinically diagnosed with moderate-to-severe axSpA (BE AGILE, BE MOBILE 1, BE MOBILE 2) or PsA (BE ACTIVE, BE OPTIMAL, BE COMPLETE). In BE MOBILE 1, patients fulfilled Assessment of SpondyloArthritis international Society (ASAS) classification criteria, without radiographic evidence of sacroiliitis per modified New York (mNY) criteria (non-radiographic (nr)-axSpA). Patients were also required to have objective inflammation (pelvis MRI showing active sacroiliitis and/or elevated C-reactive protein ≥6.0 mg/L). In BE AGILE and BE MOBILE 2, patients had radiographic (r-)axSpA (ie, ankylosing spondylitis) fulfilling mNY criteria. All patients in BE MOBILE 2 also fulfilled the ASAS classification criteria. Patients enrolled in BE ACTIVE, BE OPTIMAL and BE COMPLETE had active PsA, with symptoms for at least 6 months prior to screening. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria have been described previously. In BE

Patients were also required to have objective inflammation (pelvis MRI showing active sacroiliitis and/or elevated C-reactive protein ≥6.0 mg/L). In BE AGILE and BE MOBILE 2, patients had radiographic (r-)axSpA (ie, ankylosing spondylitis) fulfilling mNY criteria. All patients in BE MOBILE 2 also fulfilled the ASAS classification criteria. Patients enrolled in BE ACTIVE, BE OPTIMAL and BE COMPLETE had active PsA, with symptoms for at least 6 months prior to screening. Full inclusion and exclusion criteria have been described previously. In BE AGILE, BE MOBILE 1 and BE MOBILE 2, prior treatment with ≤1 TNFi was permitted, provided the patient had discontinued due to an intolerance/inadequate response (TNFi-IR) or loss of access in BE AGILE. Patients in BE ACTIVE could have previously received treatment with ≤1 TNFi; BE OPTIMAL patients were bDMARD-naïve and BE COMPLETE patients had TNFi-IR (prior treatment with one or two TNFi drugs for PsA or psoriasis). Patients were eligible to enter the OLEs if they completed the relevant feeder studies without meeting any withdrawal criteria. Study designs The studies included in this pooled safety analysis are summarised in . Full study designs have been reported previously. Following study completion or early withdrawal, all patients attended a safety follow-up visit 20 weeks after their final dose of study medication. Safety evaluations Treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were defined as adverse events (AEs) occurring after first dose of treatment, including ≤140 days after final dose (covering the 20-week follow-up period). For patients initially randomised to placebo, adalimumab (active reference arm) or other bimekizumab regimens in the feeder studies, only TEAEs occurring during treatment with bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks were included in this analysis. TEAEs were coded according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA), V.19.0. Specific terms for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) infections were not available in the MedDRA V.19.0; confirmed or suspected cases were identified by the preferred terms ‘Corona virus infection’ and ‘Coronavirus test positive’. Safety topics of interest for bimekizumab were prespecified in the study protocols, based on findings from the clinical development programme to date, potential risks generally associated with biologic immunomodulators, findings from other medicines with a related mechanism of action or comorbidities and risk factors prevalent in the study population. These included infections (serious, fungal and opportunistic), malignancies, IBD, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE), elevated liver enzyme/liver function test results, neutropenia, hypersensitivity (including anaphylactic, hypersensitivity and injection site reactions) and suicidal ideation or behaviour (SIB). Potential IBD, MACE and SIB events were adjudicated by independent committees, as were liver function test elevations (see ). Although not defined as a safety topic of interest, uveitis events (including the preferred terms ‘Autoimmune uveitis’, ‘Iridocyclitis’, ‘Iritis’ and ‘Uveitis’) were also recorded, due to the relevance of uveitis as a common extramusculoskeletal manifestation of axSpA. Statistical analyses Pooled safety data from the double-blind, placebo-controlled period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III studies (phase III pool) are reported for patients who received at least one dose of bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks or placebo during this period. Pooled safety data across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies (phase IIb/III pool) are reported up to the data-cut (July 2022) for patients who received at least one dose of bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks. Data from patients treated with bimekizumab during weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies are captured in both the phase III pool and the phase IIb/III pool. TEAEs were evaluated based on exposure-adjusted incidence rate per 100 patient-years (EAIR/100 PY). The number and percentage of patients reporting at least one occurrence of each TEAE are also reported. Data analyses were conducted using SAS V.9.4 (SAS Institute LLC). Results Patient population In the double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III studies, 586 patients with axSpA and 1111 patients with PsA received at least one dose of bimekizumab (axSpA: n=349; PsA: n=698) or placebo (axSpA: n=237; PsA: n=413). Across the phase IIb/III studies, a total of 848 patients with axSpA and 1407 patients with PsA received at least one dose of bimekizumab, with a median (minimum–maximum) total duration of exposure of 813.0 (17–1828) days in axSpA and 721.0 (12–1092) days in PsA ( ). Total exposure to bimekizumab versus placebo in weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies was 108.6 vs 73.0 PY for patients with axSpA and 218.7 vs 128.5 PY for patients with PsA. At the time of the data-cut (July 2022) across the phase IIb/III studies, total bimekizumab exposure was 2034.4 PY for patients with axSpA and 2590.8 PY for patients with PsA. Total exposure to bimekizumab versus placebo in weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies was 108.6 vs 73.0 PY for patients with axSpA and 218.7 vs 128.5 PY for patients with PsA. At the time of the data-cut (July 2022) across the phase IIb/III studies, total bimekizumab exposure was 2034.4 PY for patients with axSpA and 2590.8 PY for patients with PsA. Baseline demographics and disease characteristics were similar between the phase III (weeks 0–16) and phase IIb/III pools ( ). Compared with axSpA, patients with PsA were generally older, had a greater mean weight and a lower proportion were male, consistent with the general patient populations. As expected, patients with PsA were less likely than those with axSpA to have a history of uveitis at baseline or be taking non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs; a higher proportion had a history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus or prior TNFi use and a higher proportion were receiving conventional synthetic DMARDs (including methotrexate) or glucocorticoids at baseline. By the data-cut, 54 (6.4%) patients with axSpA and 76 (5.4%) patients with PsA had withdrawn from the studies due to AEs (based on primary reason for withdrawal). Detailed patient disposition information has been reported previously for the individual studies. Overall safety The EAIR of TEAEs decreased with longer exposure to bimekizumab ( ). During the double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III studies, the EAIR/100 PY of TEAEs for patients with axSpA was 304.2 in the bimekizumab group and 237.5 in the placebo group. For patients with PsA, the EAIR/100 PY was 245.9 in the bimekizumab group and 198.0 in the placebo group ( ). Across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies, the overall EAIR/100 PY for patients receiving bimekizumab was 136.9 for patients with axSpA and 139.6 for patients with PsA ( ). Most TEAEs were mild to moderate across all treatment periods. The EAIR of serious TEAEs increased slightly with longer bimekizumab treatment ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, EAIR/100 PY with bimekizumab versus placebo was 3.7 vs 2.8 for patients with axSpA and 5.5 vs 2.3 for patients with PsA; the overall EAIRs across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies were 5.1 (axSpA) and 6.1 (PsA) with bimekizumab ( ). The EAIR of TEAEs leading to discontinuation remained relatively stable over time ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, EAIR/100 PY with bimekizumab treatment versus placebo was 7.4 vs 6.9 for patients with axSpA and 4.6 vs 2.3 for patients with PsA; the overall EAIRs across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies were 2.7 in axSpA and 3.1 in PsA ( ). The most frequently reported TEAE with bimekizumab in the phase III double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16), was nasopharyngitis (EAIR/100 PY for axSpA: 28.1; PsA: 23.8; ). With longer exposure to bimekizumab across the phase IIb/III studies, the three most frequently reported TEAEs were SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) infection (axSpA: 7.8/100 PY; PsA: 8.8/100 PY), nasopharyngitis (axSpA: 8.2; PsA: 7.7) and upper respiratory tract infection (axSpA: 5.0; PsA: 5.6). All TEAEs occurring in ≥5% of patients across the phase IIb/III studies are presented in . The EAIRs for these TEAEs decreased with longer exposure to bimekizumab, except SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19; ). Infections The overall EAIR/100 PY of infections and infestations across the phase IIb/III studies was 53.4 in patients with axSpA and 57.5 in patients with PsA. During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, the EAIR/100 PY of serious infections was low in patients with axSpA (placebo: 1.4; bimekizumab: 0.9) and in patients with PsA (placebo: 0.0; bimekizumab: 1.4) ( ). Similar EAIRs/100 PY of serious infections were seen with longer duration of bimekizumab treatment in the phase IIb/III studies (axSpA: 1.5; PsA: 1.2; ). Fungal infections The EAIRs of fungal infections decreased with longer exposure to bimekizumab ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, the EAIR/100 PY of fungal infections with bimekizumab treatment versus placebo was 20.8 vs 0.0 in axSpA and 15.0 vs 3.1 in PsA ( ). Across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies, the cumulative EAIR of fungal infections with bimekizumab was 9.2 in both indications. In the first year of treatment with bimekizumab across the phase IIb/III studies, 38 (4.5%) patients with axSpA and 52 (3.7%) patients with PsA reported more than one fungal infection TEAE ( ). No systemic fungal infections were reported across the phase IIb/III studies. The most commonly reported fungal infections were Candida infections. Rates of other fungal infections were low ( ). No systemic fungal infections were reported across the phase IIb/III studies. The most commonly reported fungal infections were Candida infections. Rates of other fungal infections were low ( ). Candidiasis The vast majority of Candida infection TEAEs were reported as oral candidiasis ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, 13 (3.7%) patients with axSpA and 16 (2.3%) patients with PsA reported oral candidiasis with bimekizumab (EAIR/100 PY: 12.2 in axSpA; 7.4 in PsA). No cases of oral candidiasis were reported in patients with axSpA or PsA receiving placebo. The cumulative EAIR of oral candidiasis decreased with a longer duration of bimekizumab exposure: across the phase IIb/III studies, 70 (8.3%) patients with axSpA and 103 (7.3%) patients with PsA reported oral candidiasis with bimekizumab (EAIR/100 PY: 3.7 in axSpA; 4.2 in PsA). In the first year of treatment with bimekizumab across the phase IIb/III studies, 15 (1.8%) patients with axSpA and 19 (1.4%) patients with PsA reported more than one occurrence of oral candidiasis ( ). Most oral candidiasis events were mild or moderate in severity across the phase IIb/III studies. One patient in each indication experienced one severe case of oral candidiasis and one patient with axSpA had a severe case of oesophageal candidiasis; all cases resolved with standard antifungal treatment. One serious case of oropharyngeal candidiasis was reported in a patient with PsA, who was hospitalised to achieve candidiasis control after bimekizumab initiation. The infection resolved with antifungal treatment; bimekizumab was temporarily discontinued and restarted later. No other serious Candida infections were reported. Discontinuation due to oral candidiasis was low. Across all phase IIb/III studies, six (0.7%) patients with axSpA and seven (0.5%) patients with PsA permanently discontinued bimekizumab treatment due to oral candidiasis (EAIR/100 PY: 0.3 for both axSpA and PsA). Opportunistic infections No cases of active tuberculosis were reported in any study ( ). In weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, one opportunistic infection of oropharyngeal candidiasis was reported in one (0.3%) patient with axSpA receiving bimekizumab (EAIR: 0.9/100 PY). No other infections were reported as opportunistic (as predefined by company conventions) during this period. Across all treatment periods of the phase IIb/III studies, opportunistic infections occurred in 11 (1.3%) patients with axSpA (EAIR: 0.5/100 PY) and 17 (1.2%) patients with PsA (0.7/100 PY; ). The majority of opportunistic infections in the phase IIb/III studies were localised mucocutaneous fungal infections, except for one case of herpes oesophagitis in a patient with axSpA. Malignancies The EAIR of malignancies was low in the phase III double-blind treatment period and remained low with longer exposure to bimekizumab ( ; ). Excluding non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC), one (0.2%) patient with PsA had a TEAE of malignancy in weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies (placebo arm; EAIR/100 PY: 0.8). No other cases were reported in either indication during this period. Across the phase IIb/III studies, a total of five (0.6%) patients with axSpA (0.2/100 PY) and 12 (0.9%) patients with PsA (0.5/100 PY) had TEAEs of malignancy, excluding NMSC. Inflammatory bowel disease The EAIR of adjudicated definite or probable IBD remained low with longer exposure to bimekizumab ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies in axSpA, adjudicated definite or probable IBD was reported in two (0.6%) patients receiving bimekizumab (EAIR: 1.8/100 PY) and one (0.4%) receiving placebo (1.4/100 PY; ). These TEAEs were classified as Crohn’s disease in one (0.3%; 0.9/100 PY) patient on bimekizumab and ulcerative colitis in one (0.3%; 0.9/100 PY) patient on bimekizumab and one (0.4%; 1.4/100 PY) on placebo. No cases of adjudicated definite or probable IBD were reported in patients with PsA in this period. Across the phase IIb/III studies, 16 (1.9%) patients with axSpA (0.8/100 PY) and seven (0.5%) patients with PsA (0.3/100 PY) had adjudicated definite or probable IBD. These TEAEs were classified as Crohn’s disease in seven (0.8%; 0.3/100 PY) patients with axSpA and one (<0.1%; 0.0/100 PY) patient with PsA; ulcerative colitis in six (0.7%; 0.3/100 PY) patients with axSpA and two (0.1%; 0.1/100 PY) with PsA; unclassified in four (0.5%; 0.2/100 PY) patients with axSpA and four (0.3%; 0.2/100 PY) with PsA. Patients with a previous diagnosis of Crohn’s disease, ulcerative colitis or other IBD were eligible for inclusion in the studies if they had no active symptomatic disease at screening or baseline. Among patients with a prior history of IBD across the phase IIb/III studies, TEAEs of adjudicated definite or probable IBD were reported in 3/15 (20.0%) patients with axSpA and 1/13 (7.7%) patients with PsA (EAIR/100 PY: 7.7 and 3.8, respectively). EAIRs of adjudicated definite or probable IBD events in patients with no prior history of IBD were low (axSpA: 0.7; PsA: 0.2). Uveitis The EAIR of uveitis events remained low with longer exposure to bimekizumab ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies in axSpA, the EAIR/100 PY of uveitis events with bimekizumab versus placebo was 1.8 vs 15.4 ( ). In patients with a prior history of uveitis, the EAIR was lower in patients receiving bimekizumab versus placebo (6.2 vs 70.4). No cases of uveitis occurred in patients with PsA during this period. For patients with axSpA, the cumulative EAIR across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies was 1.2/100 PY. EAIR/100 PY was lower in patients with no prior history of uveitis than those with a history (0.6 vs 4.6; ). One patient with PsA and a prior history of uveitis experienced a uveitis event across the phase IIb/III studies (EAIR/100 PY: 0.0). Other safety topics of interest No adjudicated MACE TEAEs occurred in the double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III studies ( ). Across all treatment periods in the phase IIb/III studies, the overall EAIR/100 PY of adjudicated MACE with bimekizumab treatment was 0.2 in axSpA and 0.4 in PsA ( ). The EAIR of hepatic events decreased with longer exposure to bimekizumab ( ). During weeks 0–16 of the phase III studies, the EAIR/100 PY of hepatic events with bimekizumab versus placebo was 16.2 vs 9.7 in axSpA and 13.1 vs 8.7 in PsA. The cumulative EAIRs across the phase IIb/III studies were 5.9 in axSpA and 6.0 in PsA. Most hepatic TEAEs were non-serious transient elevations of liver enzymes ( ). Across the phase IIb/III studies, elevated levels of alanine transaminase (ALT) or aspartate aminotransferase (AST) >3×upper limit of normal (ULN) occurred at an EAIR/100 PY of 2.2 in axSpA and 2.3 in PsA. Elevations of ALT or AST >5×ULN occurred at an EAIR of 0.7/100 PY in both indications. The majority of cases of increased liver enzyme levels had alternative causes and were reversed with either continued treatment or shortly following discontinuation of the study medication. There were no cases of confirmed Hy’s Law (drug-induced jaundice caused by hepatocellular injury without an obstructive component) in any study. Across all treatment periods of the phase IIb/III studies, the EAIR of neutropenia TEAEs was 0.5 in axSpA and 1.4 in PsA ( ; ). Decreased neutrophil count (based on the MedDRA preferred term) was reported in two (0.2%) patients with axSpA and six (0.4%) patients with PsA (EAIR/100 PY: 0.1 and 0.2, respectively). No cases of neutropenia were associated with serious infection. No serious hypersensitivity reactions were reported in patients with axSpA across the phase IIb/III studies; one (<0.1%) patient with PsA (EAIR/100 PY: 0.0) had a serious TEAE of dermatitis ( ). There were no incidences of acute anaphylactic reactions associated with bimekizumab. The EAIR of injection site reactions was 1.2/100 PY for patients with axSpA or PsA ( ; ). No injection site reactions led to permanent discontinuation of study medication. Across the phase IIb/III studies, three (0.4%) patients with axSpA and two (0.1%) patients with PsA experienced adjudicated SIB (EAIR/100 PY: 0.12 and 0.05, respectively; ; ). There was one event adjudicated as a suicide attempt in each indication (by preferred term, axSpA: intentional self-injury; PsA: suicidal behaviour); however, no cases of completed suicide were reported in any study. All patients who experienced adjudicated SIB events had a history of depression or other psychiatric disorders (n=4) or ongoing traumatic and stressful social circumstances (n=1; suicidal ideation) as risk factors. No SIB events were considered related to study medication by the investigator, except for one serious AE of adjudicated suicidal ideation in a patient with axSpA, which was reported to be indirectly related to bimekizumab due to the impact of other non-serious drug-related AEs (oral candidiasis and genital herpes). Other confounding factors were reported, including work, personal and financial issues, disease-related pain and insomnia. Bimekizumab was discontinued and the patient withdrew from the study. This event of suicidal ideation was considered resolved by the investigator. Deaths No deaths occurred in the phase III double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16). A

This event of suicidal ideation was considered resolved by the investigator. Deaths No deaths occurred in the phase III double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16). A total of three deaths in patients with axSpA and three deaths in patients with PsA (0.1/100 PY for each indication) were reported across the phase IIb/III studies up to the data-cut (July 2022; ). In axSpA, the causes of death (reported for each patient by MedDRA V.19.0 preferred term) were cardiac arrest, cardiorespiratory arrest and road traffic accident. In PsA, the causes of death were acute myocardial infarction, sudden death and traumatic shock (following a motorcycle accident). No deaths were considered drug-related by the investigator in any study. Discussion Due to the chronic nature of axSpA and PsA, there is a need for treatments that can be used by patients long-term with sustained efficacy and tolerability. In this analysis, data were pooled by indication (axSpA and PsA, respectively) to include patients across two phase IIb studies, four phase III studies and two OLE studies. The overall incidence rate of TEAEs decreased with longer duration of bimekizumab exposure. The incidence rate of serious TEAEs increased slightly with longer duration of bimekizumab exposure; however, the types of events reported (eg, cardiovascular disorders, malignancies) were consistent with what could be expected in a population followed longer-term. The overlap of the phase III studies with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic also contributed to additional serious TEAEs, such as serious SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) infections. SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19), nasopharyngitis and upper respiratory tract infection were the most frequently reported TEAEs reported with bimekizumab 160 mg every 4 weeks, which is consistent with previous findings in patients with axSpA, PsA and with a higher dose (bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks or every 8 weeks) in psoriasis. The incidence rate of these TEAEs decreased over time, except for SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19). This may be explained by the fact that the double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III trials was not completely concurrent with the start of the pandemic. The overall rate of infections was similar in patients with axSpA and PsA across the phase IIb/III studies. The rate of serious infections remained low across all studies, regardless of the duration of bimekizumab exposure. Oral candidiasis was a commonly reported TEAE, likely due to the role of IL-17 in mucosal host defences against fungal infections (particularly those caused by Candida species) ; however, <2% of patients experienced >1 occurrence of oral candidiasis in the first year of bimekizumab treatment. Consistent with the recent findings of an expert consensus panel on the safety of bimekizumab for the treatment of plaque psoriasis, the majority of oral candidiasis TEAEs were mild to moderate in intensity and most cases resolved with standard antifungal therapy. The rate of oral candidiasis TEAEs decreased with longer exposure to bimekizumab and the rate of discontinuation due to oral candidiasis was low in patients with axSpA and PsA across the phase IIb/III studies. A lower incidence rate of oral candidiasis TEAEs was reported in both axSpA and PsA compared with safety data previously reported for psoriasis, in which patients received bimekizumab 320 mg every 4 weeks or every 8 weeks. No systemic fungal infections or cases of active tuberculosis were reported in any study. IBD is a common extramusculoskeletal manifestation of both axSpA and PsA, with a higher prevalence in patients with axSpA than those with PsA. In this pooled analysis, the rate of IBD TEAEs was slightly higher in patients with axSpA compared with patients with PsA, consistent with the expected background prevalence in both patient populations. Low rates of IBD TEAEs have been associated with anti-IL-17 therapies. Increased levels of IL-17 have been found in the gastrointestinal mucosa of patients with IBD. Inhibition of IL-17 has been suggested to worsen gut inflammation; however, the underlying pathobiology of gastrointestinal TEAEs related to IL-17i use are incompletely understood. Patients who experience gastrointestinal AEs should be monitored carefully for signs and symptoms of IBD. Another common extramusculoskeletal manifestation of spondyloarthitis is uveitis, particularly in patients with axSpA. During the double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III axSpA studies, there was a higher rate of uveitis in patients receiving placebo compared with bimekizumab. Another common extramusculoskeletal manifestation of spondyloarthitis is uveitis, particularly in patients with axSpA. During the double-blind treatment period (weeks 0–16) of the phase III axSpA studies, there was a higher rate of uveitis in patients receiving placebo compared with bimekizumab. Consistent with the higher risk of uveitis in patients with axSpA compared with PsA, one patient with PsA developed uveitis, while the rate of uveitis remained low in 25 patients with axSpA across the phase IIb/III studies. As expected, uveitis incidence rate was lower in patients without a prior history of uveitis. IL-17 has been implicated in the pathobiology of uveitis, among other inflammatory mediators. A previous analysis of uveitis in the phase IIb/III studies in axSpA suggested that IL-17A/F inhibition with bimekizumab may confer protective effects for axSpA-related uveitis; however, further investigation is needed. Most malignancy TEAEs were singular events and no specific trends were observed. The incidence rates of other safety topics of interest (adjudicated MACE, hepatic events, neutropenia, hypersensitivity reactions and adjudicated SIB) remained low across the phase IIb/III studies. Rates were similar between both axSpA and PsA, except for neutropenia, which occurred slightly more frequently in patients with PsA than axSpA. However, no difference was seen in the rate of decreased neutrophil counts. At baseline, a much higher proportion of patients with PsA were receiving concomitant methotrexate compared with axSpA (~50% vs ~5%), which has been previously associated with an increased risk of liver-related AEs. Indeed, a recent analysis of results from the phase III trials BE OPTIMAL, BE COMPLETE and the BE VITAL OLE found that incidence rates of elevated liver enzymes (3×ULN) were numerically higher in bimekizumab-treated patients with PsA who received concomitant methotrexate, compared with those who did not. However, in the current analysis, the incidence rates of hepatic TEAEs and elevated liver enzymes remained similarly low in both patients with axSpA and PsA across the phase IIb/III studies, despite the higher usage of methotrexate in patients with PsA. One patient with PsA experienced a serious hypersensitivity reaction (dermatitis); however, no anaphylactic reactions were reported across the phase IIb/III studies in axSpA or PsA. The rate of injection site reactions was low in both indications and none led to discontinuation of the study medication. Importantly, no cases of completed suicide occurred during any study. Of the three patients with axSpA and two patients with PsA who experienced an adjudicated SIB event while on bimekizumab, all had a history of psychiatric disorders or confounding life circumstances. Strengths and limitations This pooled analysis is the first to evaluate safety outcomes in patients taking bimekizumab up to and beyond 52 weeks, across the full disease spectrum of axSpA and PsA. In the phase III studies, there was a lack of a placebo control after week 16; therefore, patients were aware of receiving active treatment between weeks 16 and 52 (though patients in BE OPTIMAL did not know whether they were receiving bimekizumab or adalimumab). The data reported may not fully represent a real-world population due to the specific inclusion and exclusion criteria of the studies analysed. In real-word practice, patient populations are heterogenous and have more diverse comorbidities than the sample captured in clinical trials. The pooled study population may not be large enough to capture rare safety events. Continual monitoring and safety evaluations are ongoing in the OLE studies BE MOVING and BE VITAL; however, real-world safety reporting will be important to capture any longer-term and rare TEAEs that may occur with bimekizumab treatment. Conclusion In conclusion, bimekizumab exhibited a consistent and favourable safety profile across phase IIb/III studies in patients with axSpA and PsA, aligning with previously established safety data. This analysis revealed no new safety signals. Bimekizumab demonstrated good tolerability, with TEAE incidence rates comparable between axSpA and PsA cohorts, remaining stable over extended treatment periods. supplementary material 10.1136/rmdopen-2024-005026 online supplemental file 1
